title: Bus Tour

jokes.text: Leslie and Ben's mutual compliment standoff: 'you're the candidate' / 'you're the brilliant campaign manager' / 'but you're the cutest' / 'I love you'
jokes.setup: Ben tries to give Leslie the honor of delivering big news; they volley compliments back and forth instead of just delivering it
jokes.punchline: The exchange escalates from professional compliments to 'but you're the cutest' and then 'I love you,' completely derailing the moment
jokes.explanation: Works well because it's deeply character-specific — Leslie's over-earnestness and Ben's awkward sincerity collide in a way that feels true to both. The escalation from professional to personal to 'I love you' is well-structured. Not groundbreaking but charmingly executed.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: You should tell her.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: No, you should tell her. You're better at this stuff.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ben, you're the one who actually knows what happened.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: But you're the cutest.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I love you.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: I love you too.

jokes.text: The whole team has been waiting for the news; Ann finally asks 'Hey, were you going to tell us something?'
jokes.setup: Leslie and Ben get so wrapped up in their mutual adoration exchange that they forget to deliver the big news to the entire assembled campaign team
jokes.punchline: Ann's exasperated 'Hey, were you going to tell us something?' punctures the bubble
jokes.explanation: Classic straight-man puncture moment. Economy is great — one line does all the work. Not highly original but lands clean.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: In my victory fantasy, Obama not only attends but personally acknowledges me with 'Hey, buddy.'

jokes.text: Leslie imagines President Obama at her swearing-in: 'And I can see in the crowd President Obama smiling at me. He made it. I didn't think he would come, but he made it. Hey, buddy.'
jokes.setup: Leslie describes her fantasy of winning the city council race with increasingly grandiose imagery — cameras flashing, applause, oath
jokes.punchline: The fantasy escalates to President Obama personally attending, with Leslie addressing him as 'Hey, buddy'
jokes.explanation: This is exceptional character comedy. The joke works on multiple levels: it captures Leslie's delusional self-importance perfectly, the escalation from plausible (cameras, applause) to absurd (the President of the United States attends a city council swearing-in) is perfectly calibrated, and 'Hey, buddy' as the imagined casual greeting to Obama is the ideal punchline word — familiar, specific, and deeply funny. Only Leslie Knope would (1) assume Obama would attend AND (2) call him 'buddy.' High quotability, strong rewatch value.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I was aiming for Leslie, but Jerry got in the way. No damage done.

jokes.text: Andy's Bert Macklin investigation with dramatic 'pause' and 'play' narration of the pie-attack video
jokes.setup: Andy is narrating a serious investigation into who threw the pie, doing a dramatic pause/play commentary
jokes.punchline: 'Luckily, it only hit Jerry, so no damage was done.'
jokes.explanation: Two-layered joke: the absurdity of Andy doing a gravely serious spy-thriller narration, AND the running gag that Jerry being hit doesn't count as damage. The Jerry dismissal is the sharper punchline and lands well on its own. Andy's 'Bert Macklin' persona is great character comedy. Strong character integration — only Andy would do this.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: This is it. This is the case that's going to define my career. I'm going in.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Burt Macklin, FBI.

jokes.text: 'Also, from now on, we'll be using code names. You can address me as Eagle One. Ann, code name: Been there, done that. April is Currently doing that. Donna is It happened once in a dream. Chris, code name: If I had to pick a dude. Ben is Eagle Two.' / Ben: 'Oh, thank God.'
jokes.setup: Andy, playing secret agent Bert Macklin, assigns everyone code names for the security operation
jokes.punchline: The code names reveal Andy's romantic/sexual history with Ann ('been there, done that'), his current relationship with April ('currently doing that'), his fantasies about Donna, his hypothetical attraction to Chris ('if I had to pick a dude'), and Ben's relief at just being 'Eagle Two'
jokes.explanation: This is one of the best jokes in the episode. The structure is masterful: Andy escalates from plausible spy code names to inadvertent confessions about his entire sexual/romantic history, each name funnier than the last. The escalation is perfectly calibrated — 'been there done that' (his ex), 'currently doing that' (his wife), 'it happened once in a dream' (Donna), 'if I had to pick a dude' (Chris). Ben's 'Oh, thank God' is the perfect button — the audience has been laughing and Ben's relief at escaping the pattern is the ideal cap. Highly quotable, rich in character specificity, excellent structure.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Everyone gets a security code name. Yours is Nighthawk.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ooh, I like that.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Tom, you're Mongoose.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Cool!

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: April, you're Falcon.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: And Jerry, you're Gail.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: Why am I Gail?

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Because those are all the names of women I've slept with.

jokes.text: Ben's relieved 'Oh, thank God' upon learning his code name is merely 'Eagle Two'
jokes.setup: Andy has just assigned increasingly intimate/strange code names to everyone — Ann slept with Andy, April is currently with him, Donna appeared in a dream, Chris would be Andy's choice if he 'had to pick a dude'
jokes.punchline: Ben hears his code name is the generic 'Eagle Two' and is profoundly relieved, revealing he was dreading what his name might be
jokes.explanation: The perfect button on the code name joke. Two words — 'Oh, thank God' — that sum up Ben's character and pay off the entire escalating list. Great economy, character-specific (Ben as the straight-man normalcy anchor). Scored separately from Joke 5 because it's a distinct beat with its own comedic identity.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: So I've given everyone a sexual code name. Yours is 'The Wrangler.'

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Oh, thank God.

jokes.text: Chris's talking head: 'This has been a difficult year for me, romantically. Millicent Gergich, Ann Perkins, Andy's professor — lots of disappointment, but if I keep my body moving and my mind occupied at all times, I will avoid falling into a bottomless pit of despair.'
jokes.setup: Chris lists his romantic failures matter-of-factly
jokes.punchline: The cheerful, fitness-coach energy he applies to avoiding 'a bottomless pit of despair' — treating existential dread like a workout regimen
jokes.explanation: Excellent character comedy. Chris's specific brand of manic positivity as a coping mechanism for genuine emotional pain is both funny and surprisingly poignant. The phrase 'bottomless pit of despair' delivered in his upbeat cadence is the key comedic contrast. Strong character integration — this is uniquely Chris.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: I'll do the coffee run!

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: No, seriously, I insist. I need to do this.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: This is important to me. This matters.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: I have to be the one to get the coffee. I HAVE to.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: Please. Please let me do this. It's all I want.

jokes.text: Leslie's stump speech includes 'I will finally eliminate this city's libraries!'
jokes.setup: Leslie delivers her standard stump speech about better schools, cleaner streets, safer parks
jokes.punchline: Out of nowhere: 'And I will finally eliminate this city's libraries!' — a callback to Leslie's insane anti-library feud from the show's history
jokes.explanation: Perfect use of show mythology. The sudden swerve from legitimate policy positions to 'eliminate libraries' lands hard because it's both absurd and perfectly in-character. Strong rewatch value for fans who know the library feud backstory.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: I've been dumped seventeen times. I have a spreadsheet that tracks it. I color-code it. And I've noticed a pattern: I'm always the dumpee, never the dumper. So I've developed a system. First, I identify the warning signs. Second, I calculate the precise moment of maximum emotional vulnerability. And third, I preemptively end the relationship before they can end it. It's not healthy, but it's efficient.

jokes.text: Ben's talking head: he predicts exactly when the big laugh will come in Leslie's speech, then the cut shows the audience laughing on cue
jokes.setup: Ben brags that he knows Leslie's speech so well he can predict every beat
jokes.punchline: He narrates 'There will be a big laugh right... now' and we cut to the audience laughing exactly on cue — comedy as clockwork
jokes.explanation: Smart structural joke — using the cut to validate Ben's prediction is a clever use of the mockumentary format. It's both character comedy (Ben's nerdy mastery of campaign logistics) and meta (comedy about comedy timing). Well-constructed.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: My policy goals include: more funding for schools, better public transportation, and... we need to close all the libraries.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Wait, no. Open. We need to open all the libraries. I meant open.

jokes.text: Ben predicts 'a two-second awkward silence after Leslie does her Rodney Dangerfield impression' — cut to Leslie doing: 'I tell ya, these geese don't give me no respect. No respect at all.' — and the crowd goes dead silent
jokes.setup: Ben sets up that Leslie always tries the Dangerfield impression and it never works
jokes.punchline: The cut shows exactly the predicted silence after the impression — the joke is that Ben accurately forecasting failure makes it funnier, and the silence IS the punchline
jokes.explanation: Exceptional structural comedy. The joke works in layers: (1) Ben predicting the failure in advance removes any suspense but adds irony, (2) Leslie's Dangerfield impression is itself inherently funny in its misguided earnestness — geese + Dangerfield is a perfectly absurd combination, (3) the awkward silence is the predicted AND actual punchline, meaning the meta-layer and the object-level joke are the same thing. This is sophisticated comedy construction. High rewatch value.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Your speech is exactly four minutes and thirty-two seconds.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: How did you know that?

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: I've timed every speech you've ever given. I have a spreadsheet.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: That's either very sweet or very creepy.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: The audience will laugh here, cry here, and give you a standing ovation at exactly 4:32.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: You can't predict that.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Watch me.

jokes.text: After Leslie says 'Together we can build a better Pawnee,' the crowd goes wild and a Gloria Estefan song plays as t-shirts are shot from a cannon
jokes.setup: Leslie's speech concludes with a rallying line
jokes.punchline: The crowd erupts to Gloria Estefan's 'Get On Your Feet' and a t-shirt cannon fires — absurd spectacle for a city council race
jokes.explanation: The visual excess of a t-shirt cannon at a city council campaign event is funny in its disproportionality. Gets a laugh but is more setup for Ben's talking-head punchline.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: You're going to do that thing where you scrunch up your face and make that weird noise, aren't you?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: *scrunches up face and makes weird noise*

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Yep. There it is.

jokes.text: Ben's talking head: 'Everybody says they care about the issues, but at the end of the day, all anyone really wants is free clothing shot at them from a cannon.'
jokes.setup: The t-shirt cannon moment
jokes.punchline: Ben's deadpan cynical observation that reduces all political engagement to this primal desire
jokes.explanation: Sharp, quotable political satire delivered with perfect economy. 'Free clothing shot at them from a cannon' is a great specific phrase. The cynicism feels earned rather than cheap because the episode just showed us the crowd going wild for it.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: You know, I've been thinking about political campaigning, and I realize that voters aren't really motivated by policy or vision or integrity. No, what gets people to the polls is the promise of a free t-shirt from a cannon. That's democracy.

jokes.text: Andy re-enacting the pie trajectory by miming throwing pie at Leslie's face at close range, making her close her eyes from the incoming mime-pie
jokes.setup: Andy is doing a serious forensic reconstruction of the pie attack, using a board covered in diagrams
jokes.punchline: The 'reconstruction' involves him miming throwing something directly at Leslie's face while she instinctively flinches and closes her eyes
jokes.explanation: Physical comedy rooted in character — Andy's complete commitment to the bit and Leslie's exasperated compliance is funny. 'Don't close your eyes' is a good deadpan line. Visual-dependent but inferred clearly from transcript.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Okay Jerry, I need to recreate the pie incident for scientific accuracy.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: What? No, Andy, that's not necessary—

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Science doesn't care about your feelings, Jerry.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: This is for accuracy.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: Ow! Ow! Andy, stop!

jokes.text: Tom's plan to get the vans back: 'Let me tell you how it's gonna go down. In a few minutes, we'll walk in there, we'll give him our demands, and then, bam! I start crying.'
jokes.setup: Tom sets up a tough-negotiator persona — 'he's just playing hardball, let me tell you how it's gonna go down'
jokes.punchline: The master negotiating strategy is: Tom cries
jokes.explanation: Great misdirection. Tom's confident hustler persona setting up what seems like a scheme punchlined by the most pathetic possible negotiating tactic. The confidence of the delivery sells it — 'bam! I start crying' is perfectly timed. Strong character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Okay, so the pie comes in at this angle, it hits Jerry right in the face...

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: And then it splatters everywhere. Which means the killer had to be standing right about... here.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: Andy, what are you doing with that pie?

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Just recreating the trajectory. For science.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Okay, ready? Here it comes!

jokes.text: Tom actually cries in front of Bill: 'We need the vans, so please, give the vans, please? We need the vans.'
jokes.setup: Tom said he would cry as a strategy; now he's actually doing it
jokes.punchline: The execution is even more pathetic than advertised — he's blubbering 'please, give the vans, please'
jokes.explanation: Payoff on the setup. Works because the joke was promised and delivered — the strategy is exactly as humiliating as described. The repetition of 'we need the vans' in a whimper is a good touch.

dialogue.speaker: Tom Haverford
dialogue.line: Wait, wait, wait. We already paid for this van. What do you mean the price went up?

dialogue.speaker: Bill Butler
dialogue.line: Well, that was the pre-order price. Now that you're actually renting it, the price has adjusted.

dialogue.speaker: Tom Haverford
dialogue.line: Adjusted? It's gone up over ten times! That's not an adjustment, that's price gouging!

dialogue.speaker: Bill Butler
dialogue.line: That's just how the market works.

jokes.text: Leslie calls Nick Newport 'a real jerk' on camera — reporter then reveals he died earlier today. Leslie's official statement: 'I sad.' Then corrected to 'a bummer.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is confidently trashing Nick Newport to press
jokes.punchline: Reporter reveals he died hours ago; Leslie's flustered response collapses to 'I sad' and then the slightly better 'a bummer'
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the episode. The structure is near-perfect: (1) Leslie builds to a confident, quotable insult, (2) reporter's revelation creates maximum horror, (3) 'I sad' — not 'I am sad,' but the grammatically collapsed 'I sad' — is a perfectly observed panic response that's both relatable and absurd, (4) the 'correction' to 'a bummer' is even worse, showing her unable to recover. 'I sad' as a complete official statement is genuinely inspired. High quotability. Strong character integration — Leslie's verbal eloquence collapsing under pressure is very specifically her character.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Nick Newport is a jerk, and I'm not going to stand here and—

dialogue.speaker: Reporter
dialogue.line: I'm sorry, he just died.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: What?

jokes.text: Leslie's official statement on Nick Newport's death: 'Sad.' / 'Is that your official statement? "I sad"?' / 'No, my official statement is that is overall, a bummer.'
jokes.setup: Leslie has just learned mid-press-conference that she publicly called a man a jerk who died hours earlier; she's scrambling for a statement
jokes.punchline: Her crisis communications are 'Sad.' and then the slightly more elaborate 'that is overall, a bummer' — and the reporter's incredulous 'I sad?' is perfect
jokes.explanation: Outstanding. 'I sad' as a corrected misquote is inspired — it makes 'Sad' even funnier retroactively. Then 'overall, a bummer' as the formal upgrade is a perfect escalation-by-inadequacy. Highly quotable and specific to Leslie's character (her usually unshakeable competence crumbling in real time). 'Oof.' from someone off-screen is the ideal button.

dialogue.speaker: Reporter
dialogue.line: Ms. Knope, do you have an official statement regarding the death?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Yes. It is a tragedy.

dialogue.speaker: Reporter
dialogue.line: Can you elaborate?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: It's very sad. A person has died.

dialogue.speaker: Reporter
dialogue.line: Anything else?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: It's a real bummer.

jokes.text: The Gloria Estefan song kicks in again accidentally as Leslie tries to wrap up her statement at the Newport memorial context — campaign team immediately tries to turn it off
jokes.setup: The t-shirt cannon/Gloria Estefan routine was established as Leslie's campaign-ending spectacle
jokes.punchline: It fires at the worst possible moment — during the crisis about calling a dead man a jerk
jokes.explanation: Good use of callback — the perfectly timed speech-ender now fires at the most inappropriate moment possible. The automatic triggering of the celebration when everything has gone wrong is a solid comedic beat.

dialogue.speaker: Jen Barkley
dialogue.line: Leslie, you need to cancel all of your campaign events.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: What? Why?

dialogue.speaker: Jen Barkley
dialogue.line: Because continuing to campaign right now would be like going to the Louvre and spray-painting a mustache on the Mona Lisa.

jokes.text: TV reporter commenting on the 'jerk' quote: 'Harsh words, but this reporter does love those t-shirt cannons.'
jokes.setup: Reporter is covering the scandal of Leslie calling the dead man a jerk
jokes.punchline: Pivots to appreciating the t-shirt cannon — undercutting the gravity of the scandal with trivial enthusiasm
jokes.explanation: Good Pawnee-specific satire — the local media being distracted by something shiny is an established joke about the city. Economy is excellent.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Okay everyone, we need to organize this emergency meeting by trust order. Here's how I'm arranging you.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ben, you're here in the front. Ron, you're next to him. Tom, you're... several rows back.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: What? Several rows?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Jerry, you're in the back. Actually, you're behind the curtain.

jokes.text: Leslie: 'I need everyone to gather around me in order of how much I trust them.'
jokes.setup: Crisis meeting is called
jokes.punchline: The specific instruction to gather 'in order of how much I trust them' implies a visible hierarchy that's both controlling and funny
jokes.explanation: Deceptively well-crafted. It's one line but it reveals Leslie's entire control-freak personality — she has pre-established trust rankings for her friends, they're not equal to her, and she expects them to know and comply with the ranking. Very economical, very character-specific.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: During a crisis like this, you need to appear strong and decisive. No hemming and hawing.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: You're right. And Ben, those are some seriously impressive deltoids.

jokes.text: Leslie's analysis: 'A man has died. But that man is 98 years old, and he's an awful man. However, he is a man, and he died. Also, you called the dead man a jerk. However, he was a jerk.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is trying to process the ethical situation they're in
jokes.punchline: Her self-debate gets stuck in a loop of 'however' concessions that cancel each other out, revealing she hasn't actually resolved anything
jokes.explanation: Good character comedy — Leslie's over-analytical mind spinning in circles, her instinct to be fair constantly undermined by the fact that the man was, in fact, a jerk. The rhythm of 'however' repetitions is well-written.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I wasn't listening at all, but I disagree with whatever you just said.

jokes.text: Leslie to Ben: 'Good answer, great body.' Then to Ann: 'try to beat what he said.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is polling her team on whether to keep campaigning
jokes.punchline: She grades Ben's answer like a competition AND compliments his body in the same breath, running the meeting like a game show
jokes.explanation: Good character moment. Leslie running a crisis meeting like a panel competition show is funny, and 'great body' thrown in as a separate compliment from 'good answer' shows her romance and work brains have fully merged. Economical.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Okay, so the key to effective political strategy is to understand the nuances of partisan demographics and—you know what? I have no idea what I'm talking about. I once thought the Constitution was a type of candy.

jokes.text: April: 'I wasn't listening, but I strongly disagree with Ann.'
jokes.setup: Leslie goes around asking everyone's opinion on the crisis
jokes.punchline: April hasn't been paying attention but instantly takes a position based purely on reflexive contrarianism toward Ann
jokes.explanation: Near-perfect economy — nine words that say everything about April's character. Her hatred of Ann is so reflexive she doesn't need to know what's being debated. The construction is flawless: the honesty of 'I wasn't listening' paired with the certainty of 'but I strongly disagree' creates perfect comic tension. One of the most quotable lines in the episode.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: What's on the schedge today?

jokes.text: Andy's advice: 'If the--if the--if the guy--if-- Okay. I absolutely think that we should keep campaigning. The worst possible thing we could do would be to stop, 'cause if the campaign stops, we all stop. And stopping is certain death. Who wants a panini? Anyone? Everyone? I'm going to say everyone.'
jokes.setup: Leslie asks Andy for his opinion on the campaign crisis
jokes.punchline: Andy starts to engage seriously, gives a vaguely coherent argument, then completely pivots to offering paninis — ending on 'I'm going to say everyone' as if he's resolved the crisis
jokes.explanation: Perfect Andy moment. The false start ('if the--if the guy--'), the accidental coherence of his argument, then the total non-sequitur pivot to food, followed by decisively declaring everyone wants a panini — this captures Andy's character precisely. 'Stopping is certain death' is a great line delivered with complete sincerity.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I've got a business idea that's going to change everything. Alcoholic yogurt.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Think about it - yogurt is healthy, alcohol is fun. Together? Revolutionary.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: We'll call it 'Yogurty.' It comes in flavors like Pinot Grigio Peach and Chardonnay Vanilla.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Breakfast AND happy hour. You're welcome, America.

jokes.text: Leslie to Ann: 'There is nothing harder in the entire world than saying no to your beautiful face. But I'm going to.'
jokes.setup: Ann wants Leslie to stop campaigning
jokes.punchline: Leslie acknowledges Ann's beauty as a near-irresistible force, then overrides it with cheerful ruthlessness
jokes.explanation: Good Leslie/Ann dynamic joke — Leslie's excessive compliments of Ann are a running character trait, and using it to soften a 'no' is a clever twist. Not exceptional but well-executed.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Groffle, the awful Waffle

jokes.text: 'Okay, but we're going to do it in a classy and respectful way to get Ann off of our backs.'
jokes.setup: Leslie announces they'll campaign respectfully
jokes.punchline: Her stated reason for being classy is explicitly 'to get Ann off of our backs' — the cynical pragmatism undercuts the noble framing
jokes.explanation: Decent irony — Leslie's virtue is instrumentalized into a tactics play. Not original but functional.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: My education initiative includes this children's book I wrote called 'Groffle, the Awful Waffle.'

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: It's about Mr. Bacon, a sentient piece of bacon who teaches kids about the dangers of poor dietary choices.

jokes.text: Bill: 'Yeah, but now that I know your bad idea, I can start the company myself. With my $10,000.'
jokes.setup: Tom has pitched Yogurt Platinum as a business investment
jokes.punchline: Bill points out the obvious flaw in the pitch — he now has the idea and the money, and Tom has nothing
jokes.explanation: 'With my $10,000' is the perfect button — it recalls the running negotiation and makes the defeat complete. Bill's deadpan logic punctures Tom's hustle expertly.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I'm sorry for calling you a jerk. You're not a jerk. You're actually a really great guy, and I was wrong to say that. You're nothing like... you're nothing like Hitler.

dialogue.speaker: Newport
dialogue.line: Did you just compare me to Hitler?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: No! I said you're nothing like Hitler!

jokes.text: Ron's man-to-man negotiation with Bill consists of reading him a children's book: 'We're all your friends, said Mr. Bacon. Welcome home. The end.'
jokes.setup: Ron has sent Tom and Donna away to talk 'man to man' with the van owner, implying a more serious approach
jokes.punchline: Ron's 'man to man' strategy is reading aloud from his children's book about a waffle who crosses a syrup river — which he wrote as part of an education initiative
jokes.explanation: Excellent character comedy. The 'man to man' setup promises something gruff and Swanson-esque, but Ron pulls out a children's book — which itself is absurdly and specifically his (Mr. Bacon, a waffle, a syrup river). 'We're all your friends, said Mr. Bacon. Welcome home. The end.' delivered as a negotiating tactic is perfectly absurd. And the book has a title: 'Groffle the Awful Waffle' — which sounds exactly like a Ron Swanson children's book. Highly character-integrated.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: You have to respect dead people. It's just... it's a basic human decency thing.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I mean, obviously not Stalin or Hitler or anything, but—

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I'm not calling Nick Newport Hitler!

jokes.text: Children in the audience ask Leslie about Groffle crossing the syrup river in the same Q&A as asking about 'jerk-gate'
jokes.setup: Leslie is fielding questions at a children's event, trying to manage the Newport death scandal
jokes.punchline: Kids keep interrupting the political press questions with persistent demands to know how Groffle crossed the syrup river
jokes.explanation: Great absurdist collision — serious political crisis intercut with children demanding waffle lore. The tenacity of the kids ('did Groffle use a boat of some kind?' / 'are we to assume he swam?') competing with reporters asking about 'jerk-gate' is a brilliant juxtaposition. The escalating waffle questions are a highlight.

dialogue.speaker: Reporter
dialogue.line: So when are you going to address the serious infrastructure problems in this city?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: Well, we're working on several initiatives, but I'm also very excited about our new waffle-based monorail system.

dialogue.speaker: Reporter
dialogue.line: A waffle-based monorail? That's not a real transportation solution.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: Not with that attitude it isn't. I have the blueprints right here, and they're delicious.

jokes.text: Leslie: 'We need to be respectful of all dead people. I mean, not Stalin or Hitler, but-- I'm not calling Nick Newport Hitler.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is trying to walk back calling Newport a jerk by pivoting to general respect for the dead
jokes.punchline: Her caveat about not respecting Stalin or Hitler digs a deeper hole, and she has to explicitly deny comparing Newport to Hitler — which makes it sound more like she is
jokes.explanation: Perfect hole-digging joke structure — each word makes things worse. The Godwin's Law escalation to Hitler is both predictable in the abstract and funny in execution because Leslie genuinely isn't being malicious, she's just incapable of stopping. 'I'm not calling Nick Newport Hitler' is a great line to have to say.

dialogue.speaker: Reporter
dialogue.line: So you're telling me that on the morning of March 15th, you purchased seven waffles from the Food Court vendor at 8:47 AM, but then at 9:15 AM you only had five waffles in your possession. Where are the other two waffles?

dialogue.speaker: Reporter
dialogue.line: Did you eat them? Did someone steal them? Was there a waffle-related incident you're not telling me about?

dialogue.speaker: Reporter
dialogue.line: I have a source who says you were seen with a suspicious brown bag near the north stairwell. Can you account for your whereabouts between 9:10 and 9:20?

jokes.text: Ben's plan: apologize to Bobby, leak details to press, use it to buy time to finish the bus tour. Ann: 'No, that's not a real apology. It's just sneaky.' Ben and Leslie: [continue planning around her objection]
jokes.setup: Ben proposes a cynical political play dressed as a genuine apology
jokes.punchline: Ann identifies it immediately; everyone else continues as if she hasn't spoken
jokes.explanation: Ann as the overlooked moral voice is a recurring dynamic. Works situationally but isn't highly original.

dialogue.speaker: Bill Williamson
dialogue.line: Look, I got a van. It's not much, but it's paid off. Well, mostly paid off. Okay, the bank owns most of it. But the point is, I'm willing to let it go for the right price. And by right price, I mean any price. Seriously, make me an offer. I have a lot of debts.

jokes.text: Ron: 'Look, friend, I respect your slavish devotion to the free market, but you can't welch on a contract. Where I come from, a man's word is sacred.' Bill raises price again. Ron: 'Okay, what's your stance on pinky swears, George Washington?'
jokes.setup: Ron appeals to old-fashioned market honor and integrity
jokes.punchline: Bill immediately raises the price anyway; Ron sarcastically calls him 'George Washington' — mocking the hypocrisy of invoking honor while being dishonest
jokes.explanation: 'George Washington' as a sarcastic honorific for someone who just proved they have no honor is excellent — it's cutting and specific and delivers the irony efficiently. 'Slavish devotion to the free market' is also a great Ron Swanson phrase — he respects free markets, but even he has standards.

dialogue.speaker: TV Reporter
dialogue.line: We're getting reports of a campaign bus that has driven directly through a funeral procession.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: Oh my God.

dialogue.speaker: Ben Wyatt
dialogue.line: That was not a private meeting.

jokes.text: Bill keeps raising the price every time someone matches it — from $10,000 to $12,000 to $15,000 — and his explanation: 'For a guy whose only assets are 22 crappy white vans, it's pretty much a dream scenario, so I'm just going to ride this out, see where it takes me.'
jokes.setup: The bidding war over generic white vans has become absurd
jokes.punchline: Bill's self-aware description of his incredible luck — a man with nothing suddenly at the center of a political bidding war — delivered with serene contentment
jokes.explanation: Good minor-character comedy. Bill's philosophical acceptance of his sudden windfall is funny — he's the most at-peace person in the episode. 'Just going to ride this out, see where it takes me' is a great line for a man with 22 crappy vans.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Was I late? I couldn't find parking.

jokes.text: Leslie's campaign bus, with her face on it, slowly drives through and disrupts the Newport memorial service while the team shouts 'Back it up! Go forward! Back it up!'
jokes.setup: They tried to flee the media circus; the bus is now trapped in the middle of the memorial
jokes.punchline: The bus — with Leslie's giant face on the side — lurches back and forth through a solemn memorial service while the crew panics
jokes.explanation: Strong visual/physical comedy. The specific humiliation of a campaign bus with the candidate's face on the side disrupting a funeral is maximally embarrassing. 'I feel like he's dying all over again' from an onlooker is a great reaction line. High impact as a set piece.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I have very refined tastes. I only eat fruit that's been flown in on a private jet and has its own security detail.

jokes.text: After all the chaos of the bus lurching through the memorial, Leslie steps out and says, 'Hi... Sorry, are we late?'
jokes.setup: The bus has just caused maximum disaster at the memorial
jokes.punchline: Leslie's opener is the blandly normal 'Sorry, are we late?' — as if this was a scheduled appointment they'd perhaps slightly missed
jokes.explanation: Near-perfect comedic button on the set piece. After all the chaos, Leslie's instinct is the most socially normal, utterly inappropriate question possible. It's both a perfect character beat (Leslie's reflexive social politeness overriding the reality) and maximally economical — four words do all the work. Very high economy score.

dialogue.speaker: Jen Barkley
dialogue.line: It's not an opinion, it's an objective fact. I outsmarted you people. It's like saying the sky is blue or that I'm better than Leslie Knope. These are just things that are true.

jokes.text: Jen turns the tables on Leslie's fake apology plan by having the media there — 'You were going to use us, and we just turned the tables on you. 'Cause I'm smarter and faster. That is not a judgment. That's just a fact.'
jokes.setup: The apology was intended to be a PR move; Jen anticipated it and set a trap
jokes.punchline: 'That is not a judgment. That's just a fact.' — the deadpan certainty of self-assessment
jokes.explanation: 'That is not a judgment. That's just a fact.' is a great villain line — it's funny because of the confident certainty and because she's probably right.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: You're not going to dark emotional places. You're going to Olive Garden with someone you met on LinkedIn.

jokes.text: 'We brought a sorry for your loss fruit basket for Bobby. And it is very classy. No melon, no apples.'
jokes.setup: Leslie insists their visit was genuine, not a PR stunt
jokes.punchline: Her proof of class is the fruit basket specifications — specifically, the absence of melon and apples
jokes.explanation: This is a deeply funny line because of its specificity. The joke isn't just 'fruit basket' — it's that Leslie has a detailed hierarchy of acceptable sympathy fruit, with melon and apples clearly being the inferior, low-class options. 'No melon, no apples' as the standard of class is both absurd and somehow believable as a Leslie Knope position. Highly quotable.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: You're going to be fine. You're like the most competent person I know.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: Thanks April, that really means a lot.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: I have no idea what I'm doing. I'm pretty sure I'm failing at everything.

jokes.text: April lists everything she's done since being assigned tasks: 'I just got Champion his dog food, cleaned your house, filed that paperwork — you're officially April Ludgate Dwyer — installed a smoke detector, and now I'm back.'
jokes.setup: Chris gave April various tasks to keep busy; she's back immediately with all of them completed
jokes.punchline: She rattles through a laundry list of tasks including officially changing her legal name as if it's equivalent to buying dog food
jokes.explanation: The comedy is in the list — mundane tasks mixed with a major life milestone ('you're officially April Ludgate Dwyer') delivered in the same flat tone as 'got Champion his dog food.' April's affectless efficiency is perfectly characterized.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I'm sorry for calling your father a jerk.

dialogue.speaker: Bobby Newport
dialogue.line: Oh no, he was definitely a jerk.

jokes.text: April to Chris: 'Okay, first of all, dark places are awesome. Secondly, Ann is kind of lame, so way to dodge a bullet. And Millicent is Jerry's daughter, so two bullets.'
jokes.setup: Chris says if he's alone with his thoughts he goes to a dark place; he's devastated about losing Ann and Millicent
jokes.punchline: April's comfort is (1) endorsing dark places, (2) insulting Ann, (3) pointing out Millicent's connection to Jerry as a second disqualifier
jokes.explanation: Excellent character comedy. April's version of comfort is perfectly April — dark places ARE awesome, Ann IS lame, and the Jerry connection is a genuinely funny extra twist of the knife. The structure escalates: 'one bullet' becomes 'two bullets' with the Jerry reveal as the punchline. Highly character-integrated — only April would comfort someone this way. 'Two bullets' is a great button.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: My mom was always so supportive of me, no matter what I did.

dialogue.speaker: Bobby
dialogue.line: Yeah, well your mom looks like a thumb, and your dad's got the personality of a wet napkin.

jokes.text: April: 'You're going to be just fine.' / Chris: 'Thank you. You're right. I'll be fine.' / [Beat] / Chris to camera: 'I'm not fine. It didn't work.'
jokes.setup: April attempts to comfort Chris; he accepts it gratefully
jokes.punchline: Immediate confessional admission that the comfort had zero effect — 'It didn't work'
jokes.explanation: Perfect mockumentary joke structure. The cut to confessional is deployed brilliantly — Chris's immediate reversion to despair after accepting comfort, articulated with the clinical 'It didn't work,' is both funny and a little heartbreaking. Economy is excellent — 'I'm not fine. It didn't work.' is four words that do a lot.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Wait, Leslie wasn't the target?

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: No, it was Ben the whole time.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Ben? But... I wrote 'Ben' on his face with permanent marker!

jokes.text: April's encouragement deflation: 'You're not alone. You've got... lots of friends. Somewhere. I assume.'
jokes.setup: April has just delivered her nihilistic advice and tries to offer something resembling comfort
jokes.punchline: Each word of reassurance is progressively undermined — 'somewhere' and 'I assume' hollow it out completely; she clearly has no idea if Chris has friends
jokes.explanation: Beautiful construction — each qualifier ('somewhere,' 'I assume') strips a layer of warmth from the reassurance until nothing remains. It's April's character in its purest form: attempting human warmth and failing by honesty. Very high economy and character integration. Excellent.

dialogue.speaker: Bobby
dialogue.line: So Leslie told me this amazing story about overcoming obstacles and achieving your dreams. But you know what? I realized it's actually my story. I'm the one who overcame obstacles. I'm the one who achieved dreams. It's my story. My story!

jokes.text: Bobby Newport is playing with a tiny Wii bowling game instead of talking about his father's death
jokes.setup: Leslie comes to apologize to Bobby about calling his father a jerk
jokes.punchline: Bobby is absorbed in Wii bowling, completely unbothered by the political crisis consuming everyone around him
jokes.explanation: Character comedy — Bobby's man-child obliviousness is perfectly captured. The specificity of Wii bowling (vs. any other hobby) is good.

dialogue.speaker: Bobby Newport
dialogue.line: I'm dropping out of this race and I want you all to vote for Leslie Knope instead because she's a super, super awesome lady.

jokes.text: Bobby: 'Why don't you play with the real one?' / Leslie: 'I like this one better. The little guy looks like me. See?'
jokes.setup: Bobby offers Leslie the real Wii controller
jokes.punchline: Leslie prefers the Mii character that apparently looks like her — a moment of unexpected vanity/identification with a cartoon bowling avatar
jokes.explanation: Small but endearing — Leslie finding her digital avatar and identifying with it is both funny and humanizing. Good economy.

dialogue.speaker: Jen
dialogue.line: Look, I know you're worried about the optics, but I don't care. I'm really good at this.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: Jen, we're on opposite campaigns. This is inappropriate.

dialogue.speaker: Jen
dialogue.line: Chris, please. I've done this a hundred times. You won't regret it.

jokes.text: Bobby: 'He was, like, a million years old. And he was kind of a jerk. The only reason I did this campaign was to impress him, and he couldn't have cared less.'
jokes.setup: Leslie apologizes for calling his father a jerk
jokes.punchline: Bobby's casual confirmation — 'yeah he was kind of a jerk' — and the revelation that the entire campaign was motivated by a father who didn't care
jokes.explanation: Good character moment that's funny in its bleak honesty. 'A million years old' is a Bobby-specific way to say 98. The sad truth of his motivation is played for light comedy rather than drama.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Sewage Joe, you stole the pie from the bake sale!

dialogue.speaker: Sewage Joe
dialogue.line: Yeah, so what? I needed it for my sewage system. The pipes were clogged and I figured the filling would lubricate them real nice.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: That's... that's the most insane thing I've ever heard.

dialogue.speaker: Sewage Joe
dialogue.line: Works every time.

jokes.text: Bobby: 'Thanks, Leslie. That's a great story. I'm not 100% sure I get the point, but—' / Leslie: 'You finished this race, Bobby.'
jokes.setup: Leslie tells Bobby a heartfelt story about track and her mother
jokes.punchline: Bobby's honest admission that he didn't follow the metaphor is disarmingly sweet and funny
jokes.explanation: Bobby's innocent non-comprehension is perfect character comedy — he's not dumb exactly, just genuinely puzzled. 'I'm not 100% sure I get the point' is a great line for his character.

jokes.text: Bobby's takeaway from Leslie's emotional story: 'Your mom and my dad are both dicks.'
jokes.setup: Leslie has been guiding Bobby toward an emotional epiphany about parental pride
jokes.punchline: Bobby's version of 'getting it' is an aggressively simplified misreading of the entire story
jokes.explanation: This is the best joke in the episode. The setup is a full emotional beats sequence — Leslie telling a genuine story about maternal pride, her guiding Bobby toward the conclusion 'your dad was proud of you,' his 'now I get it.' The punchline completely demolishes the emotional arc by revealing Bobby heard a totally different story: the shared message is that both their parents were dicks. It's both a perfect Bobby character moment (his emotional intelligence is just below the threshold) and a subversive comedic reversal of everything the scene had been building. Economy is near-perfect: six words. The specificity of 'dicks' rather than 'jerks' is funnier. This is what a 9+ looks like.

jokes.text: Donna: 'I know he didn't just hit my baby!' after someone rear-ends their van — then confronts the driver
jokes.setup: The team is stuck without vans; someone hits their van
jokes.punchline: Donna's fierce maternal protectiveness over her vehicle — treating a car as 'my baby'
jokes.explanation: Classic Donna character moment — her car as her child is an established character trait. Gets a solid laugh from fans.

jokes.text: Donna: 'Don't move. Let's just stay here. For like an hour, and not let him out.' / Ron: 'This isn't right. Our girl's worked hard. We're so close.'
jokes.setup: The van negotiation has completely stalled and Bill is inside; Donna suggests a passive-aggressive stakeout instead of negotiating
jokes.punchline: Ron, who is normally the most principled man alive about not engaging with institutions, delivers a genuinely sentimental speech about Leslie — the reversal of roles is the joke
jokes.explanation: Warm moment more than pure comedy — Ron's sentimentality about Leslie is always funny because it's so rare, but here it's more touching than funny. Donna's suggestion is the more purely comic beat.

jokes.text: The witness testimony about the rear-end collision: 'It went down exactly the way my girl said it did, you mean, bald man.' / Ron's resolution: 'Well, it is, but you're an ass[bleep]. So we can settle this now. I will accept payment in van rentals.'
jokes.setup: Ron has just passionately argued that a man's word is sacred and honor matters; Bill calls him out
jokes.punchline: Ron concedes Bill's point on the abstract principle ('it is') but immediately adds 'but you're an asshole' as a separate category that overrides principle — then demands van rentals as legal settlement
jokes.explanation: Ron's principle/pragmatism split is perfectly executed. He doesn't abandon his principles — he holds them while also accepting that this person is an asshole and that asshole status creates separate categories. 'I will accept payment in van rentals' is the perfect Ron Swanson resolution — clean, direct, leveraged. Great callback payoff.

jokes.text: Ron: 'I will accept payment in van rentals.' — after engineering the fender-bender confrontation into a van acquisition
jokes.setup: Donna accuses Bill of rear-ending her; witnesses back her up; Bill is caught
jokes.punchline: Ron steps in with an ice-cold settlement offer — payment in the very vans they needed all along
jokes.explanation: Excellent resolution. The payoff works because it's both surprising and inevitable — of course Ron would engineer a situation and close it with maximum efficiency. 'I will accept payment in van rentals' is a perfectly constructed line: formal, utterly calm, and devastating. It resolves the entire subplot in one deadpan sentence. High quotability, strong character integration — this is peak Ron Swanson problem-solving.

jokes.text: Andy reviews the pie investigation board: 'Sweet kick, Leslie exits the building, and then you get hit.' Then: 'Or... Leslie wasn't the target.'
jokes.setup: Andy has been running a serious investigation into who threw the pie
jokes.punchline: His breakthrough insight: Leslie wasn't the target. Who was? Ben — which means someone had to have terrible aim to miss Leslie and hit Jerry
jokes.explanation: Good plot twist played for comedy — Andy doing a genuine detective reveal is funny because of how seriously he takes it. 'Macklin, you son of a bitch' is a great self-congratulatory line.

jokes.text: Andy realizes the pie was meant for Ben, not Leslie — meaning the assailant had terrible aim. Andy: 'Macklin, you son of a bitch.'
jokes.setup: Andy has just had a detective breakthrough
jokes.punchline: 'Macklin, you son of a bitch' — Andy congratulating his own alter-ego
jokes.explanation: Exceptional. Andy congratulating his own fictional alter-ego in the third person is a perfect cap on the Bert Macklin running gag. The self-congratulatory nature of 'you son of a bitch' directed at yourself is both absurd and completely believable from Andy. It's also a callback to the opening, giving the running gag a satisfying close. Very high quotability — this becomes one of the episode's most memorable moments.

jokes.text: Ben fired 'Sewage Joe' for sending pictures of his penis to everyone — and Sewage Joe has come to pie Ben in revenge
jokes.setup: Andy has determined the target of the pie was Ben; now he confronts the culprit
jokes.punchline: The 'assassin' is 'Sewage Joe,' who was fired for sending penis pictures to everyone — the mundane bureaucratic absurdity of this backstory
jokes.explanation: The revelation that the big mystery villain is a disgruntled government employee who sent penis pictures is a perfect Pawnee joke — the stakes collapse from 'political assassination attempt' to 'municipal HR violation.' 'Sewage Joe' is also a great name.

jokes.text: Andy to Sewage Joe: 'Oh, dude, I dare you. Please. Give me one reason to take you down. I would love nothing more—' [Joe accidentally pies Ben] / Andy: 'Oh, [bleep]. Ben, sorry.'
jokes.setup: Andy is daring Joe to try to pie him, relishing the hero moment
jokes.punchline: Joe pies Ben by accident while Andy is mid-speech; Andy immediately breaks character to apologize
jokes.explanation: Great comedic deflation. Andy has been building to his heroic moment all episode; the punchline is that the pie hits Ben anyway, and Andy's transition from action-hero posturing to sheepish 'Ben, sorry' is perfectly executed. Also completes the episode's running mystery with a satisfying comedic rather than dramatic resolution.

jokes.text: Bobby Newport at the press conference: 'A lot of people have been asking me how I feel about everything that's happened today. Well, let me tell you a little story. My dad was this amazing athlete when he was a kid...' — then proceeds to retell Leslie's story verbatim but with himself winning
jokes.setup: Bobby is about to give a press statement about his father's death
jokes.punchline: He plagiarizes Leslie's story wholesale but changes the ending so he wins the race and his dad is proud — missing the entire point of her story
jokes.explanation: Excellent callback and character comedy. Bobby steals Leslie's story — which was meant to console him — and tells it publicly as if it's his own memory, but with himself winning instead of losing, thus completely inverting the emotional meaning. 'That's just a great story that happened between me and my dad and nobody else' is Bobby at his most oblivious. The reaction 'Oh, we're dead' / 'It's over' from the campaign team lands because we understand exactly how bad this is, and it IS bad. But then it turns around — great structural use of the callback.

jokes.text: Bobby at the rally endorses Leslie: 'If you don't vote for me tomorrow, you should vote for her, because she's super, super awesome lady.'
jokes.setup: Bobby has been rambling about Leslie being great
jokes.punchline: 'Super, super awesome lady' — Bobby's maximum-effort compliment is still barely coherent
jokes.explanation: 'Super, super awesome lady' is perfectly Bobby — he's genuinely trying but his vocabulary maxes out there. The fact that this constitutes a political endorsement is both funny and touching.

jokes.text: Campaign team watches Bobby's accidental endorsement: 'Maybe we're not dead.'
jokes.setup: The team had given up after Bobby plagiarized Leslie's story
jokes.punchline: Bobby's bumbling affection accidentally saves the campaign — Ben's understatement is the perfect beat
jokes.explanation: 'Maybe we're not dead' is a great low-key reaction beat. Economy is excellent. Not the best joke but lands well.

jokes.text: Jen propositions Chris at the Newport house: 'You know, there are 30 bedrooms in this house. Bobby's in one, there's a dead guy in another, the rest are free. What do you say?'
jokes.setup: Chris has been desperately avoiding being alone with his thoughts all episode
jokes.punchline: Jen's proposition casually mentions 'there's a dead guy in another' bedroom as if it's a neutral selling point of the venue
jokes.explanation: Excellent dark comedy. The casual insertion of 'there's a dead guy in another' into what is otherwise a seduction pitch is perfectly timed and perfectly dark. Jen treating it as a neutral fact while making her case is great character work. This is dark subversive comedy at its best — the deadpan delivery of something horrifying as if it's merely logistical.

jokes.text: Chris: 'Oh! That is very flattering. But you're the opposition campaign manager. I--I couldn't do that to Leslie.' / Jen: 'Oh, for God's sake, Chris. This campaign is over. My job is done and so is yours. It's just sex. I'm very good at it.' / Chris: '...Okay.' / Jen: 'Great! Let's do it. Haven't got all day, honey.'
jokes.setup: Chris's moral objection to sleeping with the opposition
jokes.punchline: Jen's no-nonsense dispatch of his objection and 'Haven't got all day, honey' — making the whole thing feel like a business transaction
jokes.explanation: Great character comedy. Chris's earnest moral reasoning collides with Jen's pure pragmatism. 'Haven't got all day, honey' is a fantastic button — it makes the whole encounter sound like a dental appointment. 'It's just sex. I'm very good at it.' is also a great line. Jen's efficiency is a perfect foil for Chris's emotional complexity.

jokes.text: Andy gets hit by the pie meant for Ben: 'Oh, [bleep]. Ben, sorry.'
jokes.setup: Andy has challenged Sewage Joe to make a move; Joe throws the pie
jokes.punchline: The pie hits Andy — not Ben — and Andy's instinct is to apologize to Ben for failing to intercept it properly, as if it's his fault
jokes.explanation: Good physical comedy payoff to the episode-long Bert Macklin investigation. Andy getting hit again mirrors Jerry getting hit in the opening — the investigation has produced another pie victim. His apologizing to Ben ('Ben, sorry') for getting in the way of his own face is funny and character-specific.

tmdb_overview: An important person in Pawnee dies while Leslie is on a bus tour for the final day of her campaign. Meanwhile Andy investigates a security threat, and Chris finds a cure for his depression.
insight: Bus tour chaos delivers 88-point escalation comedy through 44 rapid-fire character bits.
